quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Rowan County, North Carolina (1839-1899)

No statewide civil death registration until 1913 — probate/estate files (1753-1970) are the primary substitute. A father's estate could be probated any time from his child's infancy to roughly 60 years after the child's birth; size the search window to the father's plausible lifespan, not the child's own.

entry.rationale: Target record. loc_001: no statewide death registration until 1913, so a father's estate file is the main substitute. Volume 'Rowan County, North Carolina Probate Records, 1839-1899' is full-text searchable but only about 40 percent name-indexed, so run a keyword search on Voss and variants (Vos, Voss, Foss, Fous) across the whole window rather than browsing by year. Window sized to the father's plausible lifespan (to about 1899), not Caroline's 1858 marriage. Look for heirs lists naming Caroline, possibly under her married name. The tree records only: birth 1839 Rowan County (estimated) and marriage circa 1858 Rowan County, with no parents named (log_001).

FAN item. The circa-1858 marriage record (src_001) names no parents, but the original bond or license may name a bondsman or witness, often the bride's father or brother, and gives the groom's name needed to search under her married name in estates. Check the original image, not only the index.

Dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other. It would confirm a Voss couple as a unit, supply the mother's name (her surname may be a prior married name, so not treated as settled), and by date relative to the 1839 birth corroborate a father otherwise unnamed. It does not itself prove Caroline is their child; that needs a record placing her with them.

Name-searchable United States Census 1860 and 1870 collections. Locate Caroline with her husband and Voss households nearby, a neighbor cluster likely to include her father, brother or mother, and who would then be candidates for the estate search in item 1. Households give no relationships to head in these years, so co-residence is a lead only.

Guardian bonds, orphans' court and equity court records (such as a petition to divide an estate) name a minor's father and heirs, and survive even where the estate file is not name-indexed. Caroline was a minor until about 1860. Check the FamilySearch catalog for the Rowan holdings and the NC State Archives.

Deeds between heirs, or a sale of an estate tract, recite the deceased owner and name heirs and spouses (such as Caroline and her husband), and neighbors named in boundary recitals are FAN. Window follows the father's lifespan.

Church baptism and confirmation registers (Lutheran, Reformed, Moravian and similar Rowan congregations) could name the parents of a child born in 1839. This is a lead to the family that then feeds the estate search.

Caroline's own death, burial, obituary or gravestone (after the 1858 marriage) may give her death date and age, and a family plot beside Voss burials. Her death record may name a parent, since statewide death certificates began in 1913 if she lived that long.

- **Mother:** Unknown; no marriage is recorded.
- **Searches so far:** Only the 1850 census (FamilySearch, Ancestry, MyHeritage). The 1860 census is flagged as a gap.

---

| # | ID | Type | Repository | Years | Purpose |
|---|-----|------|-----------|-------|---------|
| 1 | pli_004 | Vital record | Schuylkill FamilySearch | 1908 | Patrick's death certificate — should name parents and birthplace |
| 2 | pli_005 | Census | FamilySearch | 1860–1880 | Fills the 1860 gap; 1880 states relationships and parents' birthplaces |

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

entry.rationale: Tree/log record Michael as a farmer outside Schuylkill County in 1870 (F1) and a 'miner' in Schuylkill County in 1882 (F2, F3). The 1880 census (United States Census, 1880, name-searchable) falls between them: it shows whether he was still farming or already in the coal region, his household, and Patrick's household if nearby. Vary spellings Sheahan/Shehan/Sheehan/Shean.

FAN item. The tree records brother Patrick (I2) buying land in Schuylkill County in 1875 (Deed Book 42 p. 118, S1), seven years before Michael's 1882 appearance. This suggests a sibling pull rather than (or alongside) mining work. Examine that deed for grantor, residence and witnesses, and check Recorder of Deeds indexes for Michael as grantee or lessee. loc_001 notes laborers often leased coal-region land, so absence of a purchase is not negative.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (name-searchable) may hold baptisms of Michael's and Patrick's children, marriages and burials naming residence, previous parish and sponsors, dating arrival and linking the brothers. loc_001: Catholic registers stay with the Philadelphia Archdiocese, held at parish level, so image verification at parish may be needed.

United States Census, 1900 (name-searchable) records occupation, year of immigration/birthplace and years married, and shows whether Michael stayed a miner; confirms the later-life pattern and may reveal an earlier origin and children's birthplaces that date the move. Collection runs past the 1882 window deliberately.

Employment evidence: coal company payrolls, mine inspectors' annual reports (accident/fatality lists) and local histories of collieries, to document Michael working in a mine directly and which company hired him. Repository and holdings must be confirmed on the archive's own site; no tool result has named one yet.

Local coal-region newspapers (and a place of origin's paper) may report colliery openings or labor recruitment in 1881-82, strikes, or Sheahan family notices stating the reason for or timing of the move. Contextual evidence for the cause.

Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0): browse the Register of Wills dockets of Schuylkill and the 1870 county for a Sheahan parent (I3, unnamed in tree) or Patrick/Michael estates. Wills may mention inheritance, family land sold, or relatives in the coal region as a push or pull factor. Window sized to the parent's plausible death, not Michael's move.

Naturalization/immigration: if Michael was foreign-born, naturalization papers give arrival date and residence. loc_001 flags coal-region naturalization films as browse-only image groups, so run volume_search for Schuylkill and browse image by image.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

entry.rationale: Tree fact F3 records Michael as a Miner in Schuylkill County in 1882 (S1); F1 records only a 1870 residence in Pennsylvania (county not stated, log_001 says farmer elsewhere). The United States Census, 1880 is name-searchable and shows occupation, birthplace, household members and relationship to head, testing whether he was already mining and living with or near brother Patrick (F4: Schuylkill 1875). Search variants Sheahan, Shehan, Sheehan, Shehen.

The United States Census, 1870 is name-searchable. Pins the county and household where Michael was a farmer before the move (log_001), and whether the family farmed or mined, so the pre-move situation is documented rather than assumed. Check variant spellings and for father (I3, unnamed) and Patrick in the same household.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable. loc_001: Catholic registers sit with the Philadelphia diocese/parish, and civil registration began only in 1906, so baptisms of Michael's children, his marriage and burial are the main pre-1906 records; they name parish, sponsors and often a birthplace, which can show chain migration of kin and parish community.

The United States Census, 1900 is name-searchable and records year of immigration, years married and occupation; confirms continued mining and residence after 1882 and bounds the move date. Census collection runs past the 1882 window deliberately: later schedules testify to it.

FAN item: brother Patrick Sheahan (I2, F4: Schuylkill County in 1875) was already there seven years before Michael. His marriage, baptisms of his children and employment context in the same Church Records collection (name-searchable) may show kin sponsors, shared parish and who drew Michael to the county; this speaks to cause of the move, not Patrick's own facts.

Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950 is name-searchable. A marriage of Michael (or his children) in Schuylkill names residence, occupation and parents; the marriage entry may state birthplace and trade. Pre-1885 marriages need church records (item 3).

Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0): image browse of Schuylkill Register of Wills for Michael, Patrick and a parent Sheahan. Window sized to the creators' lifespans, not the move date. Wills/estates may name kin, a coal-company debt or leasehold, and heirs elsewhere.

Naturalization records for the coal region are browse-only image groups (loc_001); run volume_search for Schuylkill naturalization and court volumes then browse. Declarations state birthplace, arrival date and residence, which would show whether Michael came from abroad or another county and when he reached Schuylkill.

Local Schuylkill newspapers and county histories (mine hiring, colliery openings, strikes, accidents) give the industrial context for 1882 and may name Sheahan miners; contextual evidence for the work-driven cause. Mine inspector reports and colliery employment records, if surviving, are a related repository check (state archives).

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

entry.rationale: Tree F1/F2/F3 record Michael in Pennsylvania in 1870 and as a Miner in Schuylkill County in 1882; log_001 puts him as a farmer outside Schuylkill in 1870. The 1880 census falls between and shows whether he had already moved, his occupation, and his household. Also check Patrick Sheahan, who the tree (F4, deed S2) places in Schuylkill in 1875, in case Michael lived with or near him. Search Sheahan with variants Shehan, Sheehan, Shean, Sheahen.

The Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable. Per loc_001, Catholic registers sit with the parish under the Philadelphia diocese, not the county. Sacramental entries for Michael, Patrick and any wife or children can show origin, sponsors and the parish community that drew them. Use spelling variants.

FAN item. Tree source S2 records Patrick Sheahan buying land from James Kelly in Deed Book 42, p. 118 in 1875, so a presumed brother (shared parent I3) was in the county seven years before Michael. Read the deed and trace Patrick and Kelly in other deeds, as a family pull to the county. Per loc_001, laborers often leased company land, so also look for Michael's own deeds or leases. Deed Book 42 itself is a verification step against the original.

Employment evidence for the coal-mining hypothesis: colliery or mining company payrolls, mine inspectors' annual reports (which list mine accidents and employees) and county directories. Directories beyond the 1882 one in log_002 show continuity of the miner occupation and the colliery or town. Hold the repository as to be located; no tool has returned one.

Local coal-region newspapers may report colliery openings or labor recruiting around 1882, strikes and layoffs in his earlier place, and any mention of Michael or Patrick. This gives the context and possible cause (push and pull), which the other records only imply.

The County Marriages collection (starts 1885) and Civil Marriages are name-searchable. A marriage soon after 1882 may state age, birthplace, and parents and may name witnesses. Statewide death certificates 1906-1968 are name-searchable; per loc_001 civil registration began in 1906, so earlier events need church or probate. His death record may give birthplace and parent names, and may name an occupation or years in the county.

The 1900 census asks for year of immigration and months unemployed and for occupation. It records the household in the county after the move and may give years in the US, to test whether he came from abroad (a possible later emigrant origin) rather than from another county. It is the later anchor after the 1882 directory; the 1890 schedules are largely lost, so 1900 is the best later one.

The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection is browse-only (personCount 0), so browse the Schuylkill County dockets image by image. The window runs to Michael's plausible death or his parent's, not to 1882, because estate papers of Michael, Patrick or a parent (the unnamed I3) could name heirs and where they lived and worked, and may mention mining employment or an earlier home.

Naturalization petitions, if Michael or Patrick were foreign-born. Per loc_001, coal-region naturalization films are often browse-only image groups. Declarations state birthplace, arrival date and former residence, which shows whether he came from abroad or inland to reach the mines. Run volume_search before browsing.

## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

If he is already there and mining in 1880, the move predates 1882 and the date in the question needs adjusting. Search Sheahan, Sheehan, Shehan, Sheahen, Shean.

Catholic parishes stayed in the Philadelphia diocese and hold their own registers (loc_001). The name-searchable Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) could place Michael and any family in a mining-town parish, with baptisms of children and sponsors (FAN) giving first-appearance dates and fellow-parishioner miners. items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Tree facts: Patrick Flynn born ~1845 in Ireland (S1, 1850 census), father Thomas Flynn born ~1818 in Ireland, parent-child link sourced to the 1850, 1860 and 1908 death records; death 1908-03-12 Schuylkill County (S3). The question text says PA birth but the tree says Ireland, so the birthplace is itself unverified. Plan item pli_004 already covered 1860. United States Census, 1870 is name-searchable. Patrick would be about 25: look for him as head or as a household member with Thomas, noting birthplace, and test Flynn/Flinn/Flin/O'Flynn variants. Stay in Schuylkill County first, then neighboring anthracite counties since coal-region families moved between mines. 1870 does not state relationships, so infer from household order and ages.

United States Census, 1880 is name-searchable and is the first federal census to state each person's relationship to the head and the birthplaces of both parents, so it can directly place Thomas (about 62) as father in Patrick's household, or give Patrick's parents' birthplaces. Search Patrick Flynn b. ~1845 with variant spellings; verify against the original image.

United States Census, 1900 is name-searchable and gives relationship to head, birth month and year, immigration year, and (for women) number of children born, bearing on Patrick's origin and on whether Thomas was still alive (he would be ~82). The 1890 census was largely destroyed by fire, so no 1890 item is planned and 1900 is the last census before Patrick's 1908 death. A 1910 census (collection available) could show a widow, but is outside the requested scope.

Dedicated item for the marriage of Thomas Flynn to Patrick's mother. It would confirm the couple as a unit, supply her surname (the census items will name only a first name), and its date relative to ~1845 corroborates Thomas as father, though it does not alone prove Patrick is their child. Per loc_001, Catholic registers sit with the parish and the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county, and pre-1906 civil vital registration does not exist; the marriage may also have occurred in Ireland if Patrick was born there, so check any 1870-1900 census clue (wife's name, birthplaces of children) first. Any later remarriage of Thomas would need its own entry.

Patrick's own marriage record (and any Catholic marriage register entry) often states parents' names or birthplace. A baptism may not exist if he was born in Ireland ~1845 (tree) and Irish parish registers are patchy, so work back from the marriage. Census households from items 1-3 will indicate the likely year and spouse.

Patrick's own burial entry and cemetery or obituary record, dated to March 1908 (death 1908-03-12 per S3). The death certificate (pli_005) was already searched; a parish burial, cemetery record or obituary can add a stated age, birthplace and named survivors or parents. Since the baptism may be unavailable (Irish birth ~1845), this is the end-of-life route to origin. Per loc_001, sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese and some are browse-only (personCount 0), so expect an image browse.

Register of Wills (loc_001: from 1811) estate file of Thomas Flynn, whose lifespan sets the window: born ~1818, a death anywhere from 1850 to about 1905 is plausible, and the 1870/1880/1900 results will narrow it. A will or administration naming Patrick as son is direct parentage evidence. Also check Patrick's own 1908 estate for named heirs.

FAN item: record the Flynn households and neighbors on the same census pages as Patrick in 1870, 1880 and 1900, plus any sibling or in-law with a shared surname or birthplace. Siblings' baptisms, marriages and deaths naming the same parents, and neighbors who share an Irish origin, would show who Patrick's family was and where they came from. Run after items 1-3 identify his household.

| # | Item | Target | Why |

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1838-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.notes: Pennsylvania County Marriages: Martin Kearney m. Bridget (Doyle) Halloran, 1879, Schuylkill County. Confirms Bridget's second marriage and that her first married surname was Doyle, maiden name Halloran. Found incidentally while researching an unrelated question; not part of any plan.

query.description: 1900 census page image, Schuylkill County, PA - Kearney household, fertility columns

items.notes: Original 1900 census image for the Kearney household: 'Mother of how many children' = 9; 'Number of these children living' = 2. Indicates Bridget bore ~9 children, most likely during the earlier Doyle marriage, with only 2 surviving to 1900. Only one of the two, Ellen Doyle, has been identified by name so far. Roughly 7-8 children remain unidentified/undocumented.

Pennsylvania County Marriages: entry for Ellen Doyle's own marriage, with her parents recorded as John Doyle and Bridget Halloran. Independently identifies the first husband's given name as JOHN Doyle. Found incidentally; not part of any plan.

entry.rationale: Tree holds only Ellen Doyle as child; log_002 (1900 census) records Bridget as mother of 9 with 2 living, so most children probably died young and left only baptism/burial entries. Pennsylvania statewide civil birth registration began 1906 (loc_001), so Catholic baptisms are the primary birth evidence. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable; search parents John Doyle and Bridget Halloran/Holloran/Halleran/Hanlon with spelling variants. Window runs from marriage (~1855-60, Bridget b. ~1838) to Bridget's 1879 remarriage to Martin Kearney (log_001).

United States Census 1860 (name-searchable) should catch the early Doyle household, possibly with the first children. Look for John and Bridget Doyle, Irish-born, ages ~22-40 in the coal region, with Doyle children in the household.

United States Census 1870 (name-searchable) is the likeliest year to show a Doyle household with several children, including Ellen. Whether John is still alive is a lead on his death date. Try Doyle/Doil/Doyl variants and household makeup.

United States Census 1880 (name-searchable) records relationship to head: Bridget's Doyle children would appear as stepchildren in the Martin Kearney household (m. 1879 per log_001). Also catches older Doyle children living elsewhere.

Dedicated search for the marriage of John Doyle and Bridget Halloran, using Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (both name-searchable), plus church marriage entries. It dates the union and bounds the birth window for children; it does not by itself prove any child is theirs. Other places Bridget's surname may be recorded are Ellen's marriage record (log_003), which names her parents as John Doyle and Bridget Halloran.

John Doyle's death or burial entry (he predeceased the 1879 remarriage of Bridget per log_001) and burial entries for Doyle children who died young (7 of 9 did not survive to 1900 per log_002). Burial registers give ages and parents' names, and the sequence of child burials identifies siblings. Use Schuylkill County Church Records (name-searchable) and cemetery records.

Estate or administration of John Doyle (died ~1858-1879) held by the county Register of Wills from 1811 (loc_001); heirs and minor children are named, with guardianship petitions. Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0), so this is an image browse of Schuylkill dockets. Date range extends to 1900 since a guardian filing or Martin Kearney's estate could name stepchildren.

FAN and sibling-directed: marriage records of Doyle-surnamed spouses with parents John Doyle and Bridget (like Ellen's, log_003) in Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 and Civil Marriages (name-searchable). Siblings of Ellen would name the same parents; witnesses and residence suggest the 2 living children. Also Bridget Kearney's and Martin Kearney's death certificates (1906-1968 collection, name-searchable) whose informants may be living children.

United States Census 1900 and 1910 (both name-searchable). The original 1900 Kearney page (log_002) gives the 9/2 fertility counts; searching Kearney neighbors and Ellen's household for the second surviving child, and the 1910 census for the surviving siblings and for Bridget's household.

## Stagstrup Sogn, Thisted Amt, Denmark - late 1700s

For a male subject born 1779, two record classes carry parentage. Church books (kirkeboeger) hold the baptism naming both parents. The military levy rolls (laegdsruller), kept from 1789, enroll every boy under his father's name from childhood - direct evidence of the father. Danish patronymics (Nielsen = son of Niels) point to the father's given name but not the specific man. The Stagstrup register is only ~3% indexed, so plan to browse images.

The baptism entry should name both parents. loc_001 says the Stagstrup register is only ~3% indexed, so browse the church-book images (Denmark, Church Books collection, name-searchable but sparse for this parish) by date, Aug-Sep 1779. Surname Blyeberg may be a farm/byname: try variants (Blyeberg, Bliberg, Blyberg).

Per the Denmark Military Records wiki page and loc_001, levying rolls from 1788/89 list every male from birth under the father's name: direct parentage evidence for a boy aged ~10 in 1789. Search Denmark, Military Levying Rolls 1789-1861 (name-searchable) and Denmark, Military Conscription Rolls 1789-1792 (collection 2243379, per the wiki). Place fields may rank rather than filter, so verify the parish; fallback is browsing Thisted Amt rolls by volume_search.

Dedicated search for the candidate parents' marriage to each other (father's given name Niels from the patronymic; the patronymic does not identify which Niels). It would confirm the couple as a unit, supply the mother's name (possibly a prior married name if she remarried), and by its date relative to 1779 corroborate a father named only indirectly. It does not alone prove Mikkel is their child. Browse marriage entries in Stagstrup and neighbouring parishes.
Denmark Census 1787-1930 (name-searchable). The 1787 and 1801 censuses show household members and relationships, placing a boy aged ~8 or ~22 with a Niels household. Bridges baptism to levy rolls.

FAN item: baptisms of siblings (same Niels and mother) and godparents (faddere) at Mikkel's baptism. Sibling entries test the identity of the Niels; sponsors are often kin. Browse by year as the register is lightly indexed.

Objective also asks when the father died. A burial entry for Niels (father lifespan could run from 1779 to ~Y+60) gives death date and age; sized to the father's lifespan, not Mikkel's. Also covers fathers dying before 1789 levy rolls. Cover Stagstrup and parishes where levy rolls or census show the family moved.
Denmark, Probate Indexes 1674-1851 (name-searchable): a skifte for Niels names his heirs including Mikkel, giving parentage and death date. Window set by the father's plausible lifespan.

## Muhlenberg County, Kentucky — c. 1870-1890

Statewide death certificates begin 1911; no certificate can cover a death in the 1870s-1880s. County death registers (1804888) exist but the 1860s-1870s coverage is partial. For this era, **probate records are the primary death evidence**: administrator bonds name the widow or heir, estate settlements are dated, and register entries bracket the death within months. Muhlenberg County probate (1875188) survives well for the 1870s and is browse-only. Supplement with church burials, cemetery records, and census bracketing.

Likely empty; if so the death predates 1911.

Last known alive 1870 residence; pre-1911 death evidence. Kentucky, Deaths and Burials, 1843-1970 (name-searchable) includes county registers, but loc_001 says 1860s-1870s coverage is partial. Search Muhlenberg first, then Kentucky-wide for the same name variants.

Administrator bonds and settlements bracket the death within months, localize it to the county and name widow or heirs. Window runs to 1915 since estates may be filed or settled years after death.

The 1870 residence is the last known alive date. The 1880 census (lists relationship to head, with age and birthplace) and 1900 show whether Elijah, aged about 66 and 86, is still present, bracketing the death and confirming identity by household. Check mortality schedule for 1880 as well (persons who died in the prior year).

Church burial registers and cemetery records (Find a Grave, county cemetery surveys) can give a death or burial date and place when no register or probate survives (loc_001). Search Muhlenberg cemeteries for Elijah Wilkins b. c.1814.

FAN item: death certificates (1911+) and county marriages of Elijah's children name father Elijah Wilkins and his birthplace. Identify likely children from the 1870/1880 household and search Kentucky Deaths, 1911-1967 and Kentucky, County Marriages, 1797-1954 (both name-searchable) for father's name. Supports identity and bounds his death. Children's records postdate his death, so window is sized to their lifespans.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: The tree records Patrick's death 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County. loc_001 notes statewide registration began 1906, so a 1908 certificate should exist; 'Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968' is name-searchable. Certificates normally name father, mother and birthplace (informant quality must be weighed). No baptism is likely in reach because the tree and the 1850 census both give birth ca. 1845 in Ireland, outside Pennsylvania registers, so this is the subject's own death entry.

Patrick's own burial entry in the Catholic parish register (Diocese/Archdiocese of Philadelphia; registers held by parish, loc_001). Uses 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records', name-searchable. Burial entries may state age, birthplace or parents; also check cemetery records for the plot and neighbors.

Patrick's own marriage(s), 1865-1905 (age ~20 to ~60). Pennsylvania County Marriages 1885-1950, Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and the Schuylkill church collection are all name-searchable; entries may state parents' names or birthplace. Search variants Flynn/Flinn/Flin/Flyn/Fleming and Patrick/Pat/Padraig. Pre-1885 county marriage registers may be sparse, so church marriages cover the gap.

Timeline t_001 flags a 1851-1860 gap with 1860 census unsearched. United States Census, 1860 is name-searchable. Locate Patrick (age ~15) with Thomas Flynn's household to test continuity of the 1850 co-enumeration (a_004, indirect only: the 1850 census states no relationships) and identify the mother and siblings.

United States Census, 1870 (name-searchable) bridges 1860 and 1880 so continuity does not rest on name and age alone; shows whether Patrick is still in his parents' home or has formed his own household, and neighbors who may be kin.

United States Census, 1880 (name-searchable) states each person's relationship to the head and the birthplace of both parents, so it can directly state parentage for Patrick or, if Thomas or his widow lives with Patrick, for the elder household.

Dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other (Thomas Flynn, tree birth ~1818 Ireland, and an unknown wife). It would (a) confirm the couple as a unit, (b) supply the wife's surname, only if this was her first marriage, so do not call any surname found her maiden name without a companion check, and (c) by date relative to Patrick's ~1845 birth corroborate Thomas as father; it does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. Likely Irish or early Pennsylvania church; search Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages, Civil Marriages and Schuylkill church records, then note that Irish parish registers need an Ireland locality survey before planning.

Register of Wills holds probate from 1811 (loc_001), a primary parentage source naming heirs. 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' is browse-only (personCount 0), so browse Schuylkill dockets image by image. Window is sized to Thomas's lifespan (born ~1818, could die from 1850 to ~1905), not Patrick's; also check a wife's estate and Patrick's own estate after 1908.

FAN item: siblings and neighbors from the 1850 household (dwelling 84, family 91). Sibling baptisms, marriages and burials in Schuylkill County church records (name-searchable) and sibling death certificates after 1906 often name the same parents, and sponsors at Patrick's children's baptisms may be kin. This tests the parentage from records that name the parents together with the children.

Both census records and the tree place birth in Ireland, so Patrick or Thomas may have naturalized. loc_001 says coal-region naturalization films are browse-only (volume_search ~0% record-searchable); browse the Schuylkill court records. Declarations may state origin place and arrival, which would point to the Irish parish. Check volume_search before executing.

Obituary for Patrick Flynn (d. 1908-03-12) in Schuylkill County newspapers; may name surviving siblings, origin in Ireland and parents. Lead to verify against original records, not evidence by itself.

Mode: create. No plan existed for q_001 ("Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"). The only earlier plan, pl_001, belongs to q_002.

**What the tree and records already hold**
- Patrick Flynn (I1) has no FamilySearch ark, so there is no hints-review item. The project tree records his birth as ~1845 in Ireland, from the 1850 census and the Ancestry index. This conflicts with the question's "born in Pennsylvania".
- The tree records his death on 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County.
- Thomas Flynn (I2) is recorded as born ~1818 in Ireland, linked as Patrick's father on the strength of the 1850 census.
- That 1850 census lists Patrick, age 5, in Thomas's household (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, so this is indirect evidence only.
- The timeline shows an unsearched 1851-1860 gap, and the 1860 census has not been searched.
- The existing proof summary ps_001 sits at "possible" and cites only the 1850 census.
- Patrick's birth in Ireland predates any Pennsylvania register, so no baptism is likely in reach. His own death entry is therefore item pli_004, with his burial in pli_005.
- The locality entry covers Schuylkill County only. Irish parish registers would need an Ireland locality survey before they can be planned.

**Plan pl_002, in execution order (11 items, all FamilySearch except the last three)**
- pli_004: death certificate, Schuylkill, 1908. It is name-searchable and likely names the parents and birthplace.
- pli_005: church burial entry (Schuylkill church records), 1908. It is name-searchable and may state age or birthplace.
- pli_006: Patrick's own marriage(s), 1865-1905. County and civil marriages and church records are name-searchable and may name his parents.
- pli_007: 1860 census. It closes the timeline gap and tests whether Patrick stays in Thomas's household.
- pli_008: 1870 census. It bridges to 1880 so continuity does not rest on name and age alone.
- pli_009: 1880 census. It states relationships and parents' birthplaces.
- pli_010: marriage of Thomas Flynn and his wife to each other, 1835-1850. It confirms them as a couple and dates the union against Patrick's birth.
  - It does not prove Patrick is their child.
  - Any surname found for the wife is not treated as her maiden name without a companion check.
- pli_011: probate (Register of Wills), 1850-1905. It is browse-only (personCount 0), so dockets must be browsed image by image. The window is sized to Thomas's lifespan.
- pli_012: FAN item, siblings and neighbors from the 1850 household. Their baptisms, marriages and burials may name the same parents.
- pli_013: naturalization in the coal region (Schuylkill court, county courthouse), 1850-1908. It is browse-only and may give the Irish place of origin.
- pli_014: 1908 obituary in Schuylkill newspapers, as a lead to verify.

No item is a fallback for another. Hand-back: search-records for the FamilySearch items, starting with pli_004. Use search-external-sites for pli_014, the newspaper item. The probate and naturalization items (pli_011, pli_013) are browse-only images.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

entry.rationale: Review pending FamilySearch hints on ZZKR-BR1 before searching — an attached hint may already answer the question.

Tree records Bridget's birth as 1871 in Pottsville with no baptism. Pennsylvania has no civil birth registration before 1906 (loc_001), so the baptism register is the direct record. Collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (Schuylkill County Church Records) is name-searchable. Search Kerrigan with variants (Kerrican, Kerigan, Carrigan, Kerrigen) and Bridget/Bridgit/Biddy/Brigid, parents Thomas and Ellen (Burke/Bourke). Catholic infants were usually baptized within weeks, so 1871-1872 is the core window; widen slightly for a late entry. Registers are held by the parish, under the Diocese of Philadelphia.

Fallback if the name search fails (indexing may miss misspelled Irish names). The church image group 007936751 is browse-only (personCount 0, 0% record-searchable); browse image by image for Pottsville Catholic baptism entries in 1871-1872.

Registers stay with the parish or the Archdiocese of Philadelphia archives, not the county (loc_001). If FamilySearch has no coverage, request a baptismal certificate/register search from the Pottsville Catholic parishes or the archdiocesan archives; find contact details on their own sites. Parents Thomas Kerrigan and Ellen Burke were likely Irish Catholic, though denomination is unverified and should be checked.

FAN item: baptisms of Bridget's siblings (Thomas Kerrigan and Ellen as parents) reveal the family's parish, and a sibling's entry names sponsors who may also appear on Bridget's. Parents' own marriage (Thomas, born 1842 Pottsville; Ellen, born 1846 Ireland) likely 1862-1870 in the same parish; look for it here too, as it confirms the couple and parish. A marriage does not itself show Bridget is their child.

Bridget's own marriage (Pennsylvania County Marriages 1885-1950 is name-searchable; Schuylkill marriage volume 007936753, 1870-1910, is browse-only) may name her parish, age or birthplace, pointing to the church of her baptism. Baptism exists likely, so this is corroboration, not a substitute.

Thomas Kerrigan died 1898 in Pottsville per the tree; his obituary/funeral notice and cemetery record usually name the parish church, directing the register search for the family. Parent's lifespan set the window.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Supersedes pl_002/pli_006, which searched Thomas Flynn's probate for 1870-1890; a reference now suggests he died ca. 1865, which falsifies that window. The 1860 census (log_004) still has Patrick, age 15, in Thomas's household, consistent with a death after 1860. The Register of Wills holds probate from 1811 (loc_001). 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' is browse-only (personCount 0), so this is an image browse of the Schuylkill dockets for wills and administrations, not a name search. A will or letters of administration naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence. Window is set by Thomas's death (ca. 1865) with margin, since the date is only a reference's suggestion; filing can lag.

Thomas Flynn's own burial entry, the best test of the ca. 1865 death date. Sibling baptisms are attached to St. Mary's Pottsville (S5), so the family appears Catholic. Register entries often give age and origin. 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' is name-searchable. loc_001: Catholic registers sit with the parish/Diocese of Philadelphia, not the county. Search variants Flynn, Flinn, Flin, Fflynn.

Tests the death date from the other side: if Thomas is absent in 1870 and a Flynn household has a widow, Patrick (about 25) and Mary and James, that supports an 1860-1870 death and shows who the mother was. Tree survey: 1850 and 1860 censuses (S1, S2) already place Patrick with Thomas, so they are not re-requested.

Dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, Ireland) to the candidate mother, ahead of Patrick's birth ca. 1845. It confirms the couple as a unit, may give her maiden name (only if this was her first marriage; the death certificate names only the father), and its date relative to Patrick's birth corroborates the father named on the death certificate. It does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. Name-searchable: 'Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950' and 'Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900', plus church marriage registers. The tree gives Patrick's birthplace as Ireland while the question says Pennsylvania, so the marriage may be in Ireland (Irish parish registers via a separate locality survey) or in Pennsylvania.

FAN item: baptisms (S5) and marriages of siblings Mary and James Flynn, which would name both parents including the mother's name, and whose godparents or witnesses may be kin. Siblings' records supply evidence about Patrick's parents independent of his own records. Window runs to 1900 because a sibling can marry decades after Thomas's death.

Patrick (about 16-20) and James were of Civil War age during or just after Thomas's ca. 1865 death. Service, draft and any pension or dependent-mother claim can name parents or a widowed mother. Pension files are created long after the war, so the range runs to Patrick's 1908 death rather than stopping at 1870.

Patrick's own burial, obituary and marriage (the baptism may not exist because the tree puts his birth in Ireland ca. 1845, where the parish register is not in this survey). Burial and obituary of Patrick in 1908 (the death certificate informant was son-in-law James Brown) and Thomas's grave marker may group the family in one plot, giving Thomas's death year. The loc_001 notes pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery and probate records.

No item is a fallback for another. I did not plan an FS-hints item because Patrick's tree entry has no ark.

A page that fills in the Irish origin would need a separate locality survey of Ireland. None exists yet.
